newsitem.title: USA: American faces spy, illegal entry charge in N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: American faces spy, illegal entry charge in N.Korea.

text.p: North Korea has confirmed to the United States that it will charge a detained American citizen with espionage and illegal entry into the country, the State Department said on Tuesday.

North Korea said on Sunday that a U.S. citizen it named as Evan Carl Hunzike was arrested on Aug. 24 after crossing from China. The country's state news agency said it had been "proved by investigation" that he was a spy for South Korea and he would have to "take appropriate penal responsibility."
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said U.S. and North Korean officials had now discussed the case through Pyongyang's mission to the United Nations in New York.

"Now the North Koreans have indicated to us in New York that this U.S. citizen will be charged with both espionage and with illegal entry into North Korea. Those are very serious charges," Burns told a news briefing.
Both U.S. and South Korean officials have denied that the man -- whom Washington has refused to name because he has declined to sign a privacy waiver -- was spying for them.
"We are calling again upon the North Korean government to release him immediately," Burns said. "He is innocent of these charges."
He also said it was unacceptable that the Swedish Embassy, which protects U.S. interests in communist North Korea, had been unable to visit the American since Sept. 17.

"That's much too long a time in a case like this to go by without the United States government knowing ... that he's in good health, that he's not being mistreated, that he has full access within the limits ... of the North Korean legal system ... to any kind of representation," he said.
South Korea said on Monday it believed Hunzike was a China-based missionary in his mid-20s working in an area of northeast China bordering North Korea.

U.S. officials said they had no idea why he crossed into North Korea. They said they had kept quiet about the case, until it was disclosed by North Korea, in hopes that Pyongyang might be persuaded to free the man.

They had hoped that Representative Bill Richardson, a New Mexico Democrat close to the Clinton administration, might sue for his release during a planned trip to North Korea last month. But Richardson cancelled the trip when a North Korean submarine beached on the South Korean coast, provoking a major crisis.

South Korea says the submarine was landing commandos in preparation for wider military action. Of 26 North Koreans who came ashore, 22 have been killed or found dead. Pyongyang says the submarine drifted south after developing engine trouble.
The State Department said that incident was expected to be a major theme of a three-day visit Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord will pay to Seoul starting on Thursday.

"This trip is being undertaken to reflect and demonstrate our very close alliance with South Korea, the fact that we stand by South Korea in the midst of these provocations by North Korea," Burns said.

U.S. officials said Lord would again attempt to smooth raised hackles in South Korea over a remark by Secretary of State Warren Christopher, in an initial reaction to the submarine incident, that "all parties" should show restraint.

Officials say Christopher did not intend the remark, and held North Korea entirely to blame for the incident, but South Korean media have taken it as evidence that Washington is trying to appease North Korea.
